seo.title: Karmic tail 21 16 22 compatibility: The World, The Tower, The Fool
seo.description: Karmic tail 21 16 22 compatibility: a couple who enter through The World, pass The Tower and must learn The Fool, read through Tevye and Golde's story.

title: Karmic tail 21-16-22 in compatibility: the fiddler on the roof
short: In a couple with the karmic tail 21-16-22, the entry to the task is The World, the last card of the deck; the middle is The Tower; and the main task is The Fool, the card with which the tarot journey only begins. The answer to the riddle is unexpected: this couple starts with a ready-made world for two, goes through its collapse, and learns what the ready-made world never could — to keep their balance without walls, travelling light, choosing each other again.

sections.h2: The fiddler on the roof: the whole tail in one monologue
paragraphs: The most accurate portrait of this tail was written long before compatibility calculators. For twenty years, from 1894 to 1914, Sholem Aleichem published the monologues of Tevye the Dairyman — a village poor man who carts cheese and butter to the summer folk of Boiberik and the townsfolk of Yehupetz, argues with God in quotations from Scripture and marries off his daughters. In 1964 these stories became the Broadway musical Fiddler on the Roof (book by Joseph Stein, music by Jerry Bock, lyrics by Sheldon Harnick); in 1971 Norman Jewison made it into a film. In Russia the same story is also known through Grigory Gorin's play Pominalnaya molitva ("A Memorial Prayer"), staged by Mark Zakharov at the Lenkom theatre in 1989 with Yevgeny Leonov as Tevye.

The title was suggested by Marc Chagall's paintings, where a fiddler plays above the roofs of a shtetl. And the musical opens with Tevye's monologue — read it next to the three cards, and the whole of the tail 21-16-22 is in it, together with the couple's centre:

"A fiddler on the roof. Sounds crazy, no? But in our little village of Anatevka, you might say every one of us is a fiddler on the roof, trying to scratch out a pleasant, simple tune without breaking his neck. <…> You may ask, why do we stay up there if it's so dangerous? We stay because Anatevka is our home. And how do we keep our balance? That I can tell you in a word: Tradition!" (Here and below, lines from the musical and the film are quoted in the original English.)

Tradition is The World, the entry to the task: a whole way of life in which, as Tevye puts it, "everyone knows who he is and what God expects him to do". The roof is The Tower, the middle: a house that holds until it is shaken. The fiddler is The Fool, the main task: to play at the very edge and not fall. And the balance is Justice, which stands in the centre for every couple with this tail. The whole musical is about what happens when tradition stops keeping the balance and the roof becomes the only place left to stand.

sections.h2: Entry to the task — The World: twenty-five years without one question
paragraphs: Tevye and Golde married the way it was done: they were matched. "The first time I met you was on our wedding day," he reminds her twenty-five years later. Their parents told them back then that they would learn to love each other. Nobody spoke of love again: there was the house, five daughters, the cow, the Sabbath candles — there was a world in which everything stood in its place.

The World at the entry to a couple's tail is exactly this wish to have a whole. For Lisovskaya, the entry point is what the two want together: their agreements, their "common language". For a 21-16-22 couple the common language is a way of life. Such two assemble the picture of their life quickly and completely: how they celebrate holidays, where they go in summer, who handles the money, what the house will be like, who the children will become. From outside this often looks like the ideal couple — settled, understandable, "doing it properly". Inside it is real peace: there is no need to negotiate every day, because everything has already been agreed.

But the entry point sits on the line of tasks, and the same wish turns into resistance. A whole world has nowhere to grow. New friends, new ideas, a new job have to pass through customs: "that's not how we do things". The partner is gradually adjusted to fit the shared picture, and the picture cannot be argued with — it belongs to both. For The World reversed, Waite gives four words that read like an inventory of such a flat: "Inertia, fixity, stagnation, permanence." Wen calls The World "the supreme balance between good and evil" — and Tevye also speaks of balance, only in his case tradition is what holds it.

What this world is made of can be heard in Tevye's best-known song, "If I Were a Rich Man". He dreams of a big house with rooms by the dozen, where one staircase only goes up, another, even longer, only comes down, and a third leads nowhere, just for show. In the couple's tail The World is built from the partners' personal tails as The Moon plus The Empress, a dream plus a house (more on this in the section on the calculation). This couple's world is exactly such a house: built from a dream, full, beautiful — and with a staircase that leads nowhere.

sections.h2: Middle of the task — The Tower: a world that falls stone by stone
paragraphs: In Anatevka the roof cracks not from lightning but from the daughters. The eldest, Tzeitel, refuses the rich butcher she has been matched with and gives her word to a poor tailor — herself, with no matchmaker. The second, Hodel, follows the revolutionary Perchik to Siberia. The third, Chava, marries a Russian boy, Fyedka, and here Tevye, who has weighed every decision all his life, says: "If I try and bend that far, I'll break." Then a pogrom bursts into Tzeitel's wedding, and at the end the constable brings an order: in Sholem Aleichem the Jews are given three days to sell everything and leave the village.

In Waite's historical description of The Tower there is a phrase that fits this story literally: "It is assuredly a card of confusion." The Tower's blow is not necessarily loud. More often it is the day when the finished picture stops matching life: one of the two is still following the old map, the other is already following the terrain.

For a 21-16-22 couple the middle of the path is made of such days. A move that cancelled everything. A job that stopped being a support. A child who chose something other than what was planned for them. A partner who turned out not to be the person the other had imagined — but someone alive and inconvenient. This is not a forecast of events: the middle of the tail describes how the couple go from their wish to their task — through the collapse of the picture, not along a smooth road.

In the plus, The Tower pulls the couple together. When the roof cracks, it turns out the two know how to hold: one offers a shoulder while the other cannot stand, decisions are made quickly and without unnecessary words, and in place of the imagined partner the real one finally appears. In the minus, the same blow drives them apart: each saves their own part of the world and looks their own way, and in the heat of the moment someone says "then go".

The musical has a scene that shows how The Tower enters such a couple from the inside. To break off the match with the butcher, Tevye wakes Golde in the middle of the night and tells her an invented nightmare: her grandmother has come from the other world to bless the tailor, and the butcher's late wife threatens terrible revenge. Golde interprets the dream and herself demands that their daughter marry the tailor. In Waite's divinatory list for The Tower, the word deception stands between disgrace and ruin, but this deception is a special one. In this house the shared picture cannot be argued with, so it is changed in secret: the old agreement is broken not head-on but through the language in which the wife speaks to the world. This is the hidden mechanism of a couple with The World at the entry: when the picture cannot be challenged, changes arrive in disguise.

The Tower in this story has a second half too. At the end, Golde sweeps the floor of the house they are leaving forever: "I don't want to leave a dirty house!" The walls go, but the care for them stays.

sections.h2: Main task — The Fool: "You're a fool!" — "I know"
paragraphs: In the middle of the collapse, when Hodel is already engaged to Perchik without asking her parents, Tevye comes to his wife and says: "It's a new world, Golde. A new world. Love." And he asks the question he has not asked in twenty-five years: "Do you love me?"

At first Golde does not understand the question, then decides her husband has indigestion and sends him to lie down. Then she snaps: "You're a fool!" — and Tevye answers: "I know." And asks again. So she lists the twenty-five years: she washed his clothes, cooked his meals, cleaned his house, gave him children, milked the cow, fought with him, starved with him — if that's not love, what is? The song ends on the thought that it doesn't change a thing, but after twenty-five years it's nice to know.

Here is the main task of the tail 21-16-22, told in a single scene. **The Fool as the main task is not carelessness to be defeated but a beginner's question that the couple must learn to ask after everything.** "You're a fool!" — "I know": only someone willing to play the fool asks about what "goes without saying". Lisovskaya reads a couple's main task mostly through the minus, and among The Fool's minuses she lists an undefined status of the relationship. Tevye and Golde's status is more firmly defined than anyone's: matched, married, five daughters. Only the main thing is undefined — whether they chose each other. Formally everything is clear, yet it has never once been said aloud.

This minus has other faces as well. A lightness that turns into flight at the first serious step. Rules that one partner strictly holds the other to and breaks themselves. A quarrel after which it is easier to drive off than to stay. Tevye knows this too: in Sholem Aleichem, Chava steps out to meet him on a forest road and grabs the horse by the bridle, and he whips up the horse and drives away — and all the way home it seems to him that she is running after the cart.

The Fool's plus is the other side of the same coin: the ability to start from zero, humour when it is frightening, trust without checking. Tevye goes broke, loses his home, argues with God and keeps joking; that humour is his safety margin. The Fool is the card of the road travelled light, and that is its lesson for a couple who came in through a whole world: **the most important thing in a union cannot be inherited along with the way of life — it is chosen, again and aloud.**

sections.h2: "Get thee out": a road that cannot be walked alone
paragraphs: The last chapter of Tevye the Dairyman is called "Lekh-Lekho", usually rendered in English as "Get Thee Out". These are the first words with which God addresses Abraham. Tevye retells them his own way: "Get out, Tevye, 'from your country and from your birthplace'… 'to the land that I will show you' — wherever your eyes may lead!" And to his daughter, who asks where they are to go now, he answers: "When God appeared to our father Abraham and told him, 'Get thee out of thy country,' did Abraham ask where to?" (Sholem Aleichem is quoted in our translation.)

This is The Fool: the one who leaves without knowing where. But in the book Tevye hears "Get thee out" alone. Golde has died earlier, in the chapter "Tevye Leaves for the Land of Israel", and her last words are about caring for him: "I'm dying, Tevye — who will cook your supper?" And Tevye, not yet believing it, answers with a saying: "Golde, you've been faithful to me all these years — will you leave me a fool in my old age?" In the Russian translation the Fool's word sounds even here — v durakakh, "left a fool" — beside his dying wife, just as in the musical it will sound in the song about love.

The musical changed this fate: two people leave Anatevka. Tevye and Golde set off for America with their youngest daughters. In the film Golde calls after Chava, whom her father has forbidden them even to mention: "We will be staying with Uncle Avram!" — and so leaves her daughter an address. Tevye grumbles: "The whole world has to know our business!" The uncle the couple are going to bears the same name as the first man who heard "Get thee out".

The numbers of the tail say the same. **In a personal matrix the tail 21-16-22 is impossible:** for a single person the entry to the tail equals the karmic task plus the centre of the chart, and with The Fool as the karmic task, The World at the entry cannot come out with any centre. From The World to The Fool there is no way alone — only together. Sholem Aleichem sent Tevye down the road alone; the musical sent a couple, and that is the only version this tail allows.
At the end, as the family sets off, the fiddler begins to play, Tevye beckons with a nod, and the fiddler follows them out of the village. There is no roof any more, but the music leaves with them.

sections.h2: Justice in the centre: "on the other hand"
paragraphs: Every couple with the tail 21-16-22 has 8, Justice, in the centre. This is no accident: such couples are always formed from the personal tails 18-3-12 and 3-13-10, and the centres that go with these tails are always 6 and 20; 6 + 20 = 26, 2 + 6 = 8. The centre in a couple's matrix is the atmosphere between the two — what is inside and not for show.

Tevye is Justice in the flesh, and Sholem Aleichem shows it in the very first story. Tevye stands on the veranda of the rich and turns to God: "You are great, merciful and just! What kind of order is it, that to one You give everything and to another — nothing?" And straight away, without drawing breath: "But on the other hand, I think, you are a great fool, Tevye!" The scales and The Fool in a single sentence: the weighing ends with the one who weighs calling himself a fool.

The musical turned "on the other hand" into a refrain. Motel the tailor asks for Tzeitel's hand: on the other hand, he has absolutely nothing; on the other hand, things could never get worse for him, only better. Hodel gets engaged without a matchmaker: "On the other hand, our old ways were once new, weren't they?" And when Chava marries an outsider: "On the other hand… No! There is no other hand!"

This is the atmosphere of this couple. In the plus it is honest: everything is discussed, duties are shared equally, and Lisovskaya also sees in Justice at the centre respect for the traditions of both families and a wish to make the relationship official and proper. Weighing keeps the house in balance, the way tradition keeps the fiddler. In the minus, the scales lose their second pan. Everything is measured by one's own yardstick, responsibility turns into control, and a moment comes when one of the two says "there is no other hand". Waite's divinatory list for Justice reversed includes "bigotry, bias, excessive severity" — that is what scales with one pan look like.

The musical shows where this couple's second pan is. Tevye has forbidden any talk of Chava — Golde shouts her an address as they part. Tevye has turned away from his daughter — and at once prompts Tzeitel to add: "God be with you." **A couple's justice rests not on one person doing the weighing but on two: when one of them has no other hand, the partner holds it.**

sections.h2: The couple's values — The Lovers: Adam and Eve had a matchmaker too
paragraphs: "The couple's values" is the spiritual purpose, the path the two are to walk together. For every couple with this tail it holds 6, The Lovers. A couple who enter the task through a ready-made way of life end up valuing not the way of life but the choice.

Tevye put this into words as well. Blessing Hodel and Perchik, who got engaged without a matchmaker, he argues with himself: "On the other hand, did Adam and Eve have a matchmaker? Yes, they did. And it seems these two have the same matchmaker." The joke is precise: nobody matched the first couple in the world except the one who created them both — and a union by love turns out to be not a breach of order but its beginning.

For a 21-16-22 couple this means something simple. A union that began as a given holds because it is chosen. Tevye and Golde's marriage was arranged by their parents; their value is a question asked twenty-five years later and the answer "I suppose I do". The tail shows the road; The Lovers show what the road is walked for.

sections.h2: What Waite and Wen saw: confusion, a bundle and the edge of a cliff
paragraphs: In the books on tarot this tail has several clues that match Tevye's story with surprising precision.

Waite calls The Tower "a card of confusion", and of The Fool he writes that this card "reverses, under high warrants, all the confusions that have preceded it". Waite meant the muddle of the commentators, but the word is the same, and in a couple's tail it works literally: The Fool stands right after The Tower and answers its confusion. In Anatevka the confusion ended not with a new rule but with a simple question: "Do you love me?"

Wen describes The Fool with a bundle over one shoulder holding "all his earthly possessions". In Sholem Aleichem, before leaving, Tevye walks into the emptied house: "On the floor — bundles, bundles, bundles! A cat sits on the stove ledge like an orphan." And Chava, on hearing of the expulsion, decides to share it with her family and brings her own bundle, "tied up in a red kerchief": "Our exile is her exile."

Waite's Fool stands at the edge of a precipice and looks not down but at the sky, and the edge does not frighten him — "it is as if angels were waiting to uphold him, if it came about that he leaped from the height". This is the same fiddler on the roof: a man who plays at the edge and does not fall, because he is not looking into the abyss.

Wen explains The Fool reversed with a psalm: "The fool says in his heart, 'There is no God.'" Tevye is a Fool of another kind. He is ruined, driven out, reproaches God ("Why have You fastened on Tevye?"), yet never once says there is no God. For a couple the difference is the same: there is a lightness that does not care, and a lightness that argues but does not walk away.

Waite describes The Lovers as Adam and Eve in paradise and writes that his card replaced "the old card of marriage", which showed "father and mother, with their child placed between them". Tevye's joke about the matchmaker argues with exactly this: the old card of marriage is a family that was arranged; the new one is two people who chose.
And finally — a coincidence now, not a clue: the first Tevye on Broadway in 1964 was Zero Mostel. Zero — and zero, for Waite, is the number of The Fool.

A couple's tail is not derived from its two outer numbers: each point of the couple is the sum of the matching points of two personal matrices, reduced to 22. A person born on 05.12.1975 has the personal karmic tail 18-3-12 (The Moon, The Empress, The Hanged Man) and centre 6. A person born on 04.01.1976 has the tail 3-13-10 (The Empress, Death, The Wheel of Fortune) and centre 20. Add point to point:

head: Point

How it is derived
rows: 12 + 10: The Hanged Man and The Wheel of Fortune

paragraphs: The couple's values for these dates are 6, The Lovers. And this is not one possibility among many but the only one: a couple's tail 21-16-22 is formed only from the personal tails 18-3-12 and 3-13-10, so such couples always have 8 in the centre and 6 in the values. It occurs in about one couple in 3,742 (0.027%) — 94th place out of 97 couple tails.

The middle here is not the reduced sum of the outer numbers: 21 + 22 = 43, 4 + 3 = 7. By the logic of a single person, The Chariot would stand between The World and The Fool — a vehicle that carries one to the goal. In a couple this place holds The Tower, built from the partners' middles, 3 + 13 = 16. In a personal matrix such a middle is impossible. This couple are not carried from their world onto the road — they tumble out onto it.

What follows is our reading of the arithmetic. The Empress stands in the personal tails of both partners, in the middle for one and at the entry for the other, and in the couple's tail she goes into two cards at once: with The Moon she gives The World, with Death she gives The Tower. The house is this couple's common material: their world is built from it, and it is also what collapses in the middle of the path. The Fool, in turn, is made of The Hanged Man and The Wheel of Fortune — of the ability to hang in uncertainty and a turn of fate. Tevye describes this mechanism himself: "if God wants the wheel to turn the other way, everything flies to the devil", and then — "now up, now down!" The main task is born where the two stop holding on to the wheel and agree to hang for a while as it turns.

sections.h2: How a couple live the tail 21-16-22: the circle and the way out
paragraphs: The circle in the minus looks like this. The two quickly build a shared world and settle down: everything is agreed. The world closes up — anything new has to pass through customs, the main thing goes unsaid because it "goes without saying". Then life shifts one wall, and it turns out that the shared picture cannot be argued with and changing it openly is frightening. Changes arrive in disguise, quarrels arrive suddenly, in trouble each saves their own part of the house. When it comes to a serious step, someone turns the cart around. And the question everything was for remains unasked.

The way out is the same path in the plus. The world stays, but becomes portable: whatever can be carried in a bundle — habits, jokes, rituals, a common language. The Tower stops being a verdict: the couple discover that they can hold together. The Fool turns from flight into a road: the two choose each other aloud and travel on light, and the fiddler follows.
What helps along the way:

ul: **Ask Tevye's question.** From time to time ask directly: "Do you love me?", "Would you choose this again?" — and answer not with a list of chores but with words.
**Tell custom from balance.** A custom is a tool, not a roof. Once a year, review the couple's rules: which still hold, and which are held up by inertia alone.
**Keep the second pan.** In an argument, first restate the partner's point so well that they agree with the restatement, and only then object.
**Build a portable world.** Cherish what does not depend on walls: shared jokes, songs, rituals, private words. They can be taken anywhere.
**In trouble, together first.** When a wall falls, don't argue about whose wall it was; sort that out later.
**Practise zero on a small scale.** A new place, a new project, a week without a plan — together, so that the big start from zero is not the first one.
**Don't turn the cart around.** When the urge comes to run from a hard conversation, say so aloud and stay.

**Entry to the task — 21, The World.** The couple want a whole world for two: a shared way of life, a shared picture of life where everything has its place. Everything starts from this wish — and the couple run up against the same wish when life asks for change.

**Middle of the task — 16, The Tower.** The path runs through moments when the finished picture stops matching life: the order collapses, the imagined image of the partner collapses. Here The Tower does not promise misfortune; it describes how the couple walk their path.

**Main task — 22, The Fool.** To learn to live without a ready-made world: to start from zero, to trust without checking, to joke when it is frightening, and to choose each other not by custom but of their own free will.

faq.q: What does the karmic tail 21-16-22 mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is a couple's tail in which the entry to the task is The World (21), the middle is The Tower (16), and the main task is The Fool (22). The couple start with the wish for a whole shared world, go through the collapse of the finished picture and learn the main thing: to live without the ready-made, to choose each other again, to trust and to start from zero.

faq.q: Does The Tower in the middle mean the couple will split up?
faq.a: No. The tail does not predict events. The Tower in the middle describes how the couple walk their path: through moments when the finished picture stops matching life. In the plus such moments pull the couple together, in the minus they drive them into separate corners, and which way it goes is decided by the two of them, not by the card.

The middle of a couple's tail is not derived from the outer numbers. It is made from the middles of the partners' personal tails: 3 + 13 = 16. Reducing the outer numbers would give 7, The Chariot, but in a couple this place holds The Tower, and no personal matrix has such a middle.

faq.q: Can the tail 21-16-22 appear in a personal matrix?
faq.a: No. In a personal matrix the entry to the tail equals the karmic task plus the centre of the chart, and with The Fool as the karmic task an entry of 21 cannot come out with any centre. This tail exists only for couples.

faq.q: Are there couple tails made of the same numbers in a different order?
faq.a: No. From the numbers 21, 16 and 22 a couple's tail comes out in only one order — 21-16-22 — so there is nothing to confuse it with.

About one couple in 3,742 (0.027%), 94th place out of 97 couple tails. All such couples are formed from the personal tails 18-3-12 and 3-13-10, so they always have Justice in the centre and The Lovers in their values.
